claim: Relevant prospective moments arise intermittently, while most of the time is filled with irrelevant events, or noise, that constantly bombard our sensory systems.
source: Relevant prospective moments arise intermittently, while most of the time is filled with irrelevant events, or noise, that constantly bombard our sensory systems.
evidence: This is a general statement about the nature of sensory experience, drawing from established understanding of how sensory systems process information.

claim: Anticipating a few key moments necessitates disregarding what lies between the present and the future – the noise.
source: Thus, anticipating a few key moments necessitates disregarding what lies between the present and the future – the noise.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the functional requirements of temporal anticipation, based on logical inference from the nature of the task.

claim: Neural power within the alpha-beta band range fluctuates over time, accurately identifying the marked locations on a sub-second scale.
source: Our research revealed a unique neural-power modulation pattern for sequential temporal anticipation: neural power within the alpha-beta band range fluctuates over time, accurately identifying the marked locations on a sub-second scale and correlating with tone detection performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from EEG recordings and modulation spectrum analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: Neural power modulation in the alpha-beta band correlates with tone detection performance.
source: Our research revealed a unique neural-power modulation pattern for sequential temporal anticipation: neural power within the alpha-beta band range fluctuates over time, accurately identifying the marked locations on a sub-second scale and correlating with tone detection performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analyses between neural measurements and behavioral performance shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The hidden dynamics of the RNNs mirrored the neural modulations observed in human participants.
source: The hidden dynamics of the RNNs mirrored the neural modulations, and additional analyses and perturbations on the RNNs indicated that the neural power modulations in the alpha-beta band resulted from selective suppression of irrelevant noise periods and heightened sensitivity to anticipated temporal locations.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of RNN hidden activities with neural data, as shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Neural power modulations in the alpha-beta band result from selective suppression of irrelevant noise periods and heightened sensitivity to anticipated temporal locations.
source: The hidden dynamics of the RNNs mirrored the neural modulations, and additional analyses and perturbations on the RNNs indicated that the neural power modulations in the alpha-beta band resulted from selective suppression of irrelevant noise periods and heightened sensitivity to anticipated temporal locations.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNN modeling results, particularly the uniform distribution experiment shown in Figure 4F-G.

claim: Sequential temporal anticipation involves a process of dynamic gain control.
source: Our behavioral, neural, and modeling findings collectively indicate that sequential temporal anticipation involves a process of dynamic gain control: anticipating a few significant moments involves actively disregarding irrelevant events that frequently occur.
evidence: This is a synthesis claim based on the combined neural and modeling findings presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Anticipating a few significant moments involves actively disregarding irrelevant events that frequently occur.
source: Our behavioral, neural, and modeling findings collectively indicate that sequential temporal anticipation involves a process of dynamic gain control: anticipating a few significant moments involves actively disregarding irrelevant events that frequently occur.
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNN modeling results showing suppression of noise periods outside temporal locations.

claim: Sequential temporal anticipation offers a more thorough understanding of temporal anticipation compared to previous studies that only anticipate a single target event.
source: In this sense, sequential temporal anticipation offers a more thorough understanding of temporal anticipation compared to previous studies that only anticipate a single target event.
evidence: This is a comparative claim about the scope of the current study relative to previous work, based on logical inference.

claim: Previous studies of temporal anticipation primarily focus on situations where only the timing of a single target event is anticipated.
source: However, this dynamic, contiguous process of temporal anticipation is not fully captured by previous studies, which primarily focus on situations where only the timing of a single target event is anticipated. Examples of these situations include anticipating the onset of an event, estimating the duration of an interval, or predicting the end of a lasting event (Coull and Nobre, 1998; Martens and Johnson, 2005; Niemi and Näätänen, 1981; Nobre et al., 2007; Christina Nobre, 2001; Samaha et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on temporal anticipation.

claim: When rhythmic sequences are presented, temporal anticipation can be based on neural oscillatory patterns that are entrained by these sequences that provide external timing cues.
source: When rhythmic sequences are presented, temporal anticipation can be based on neural oscillatory patterns that are entrained by these sequences that provide external timing cues (Arnal et al., 2015; Doelling et al., 2019; Doelling and Poeppel, 2015; Henry et al., 2014; Henry and Obleser, 2012; Herrmann et al., 2016; Morillon et al., 2014; Morillon et al., 2016; Spaak et al., 2014; Ten Oever et al., 2017; van Bree et al., 2021; Tal et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research on neural entrainment.

claim: The timing of an upcoming event can be predicted by using the previous event as a temporal cue and estimating the duration of a fixed interval.
source: For example, the timing of an upcoming event can be predicted by using the previous event as a temporal cue and estimating the duration of a fixed interval.
evidence: This is a general statement about temporal prediction mechanisms, drawing from established knowledge in the field.

claim: Past research has indirectly studied temporal anticipation by observing its effects on behavioral and neural responses to sensory events.
source: Past research has indirectly studied temporal anticipation by observing its effects on behavioral and neural responses to sensory events (Grabenhorst et al., 2019; Tavano et al., 2019) and by employing an encoding framework (Herbst et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research methodologies.

claim: The current study directly investigates how the brain internally manages sequential temporal anticipation within flat white noise.
source: However, here, we directly investigate how the brain internally manages sequential temporal anticipation within flat white noise.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological approach of the current study.

claim: RNNs are flexible to train and can be tested on variations of the current behavioral task to test different hypotheses.
source: One advantage of employing neural network models is that RNNs are flexible to train and can be tested on variations of the current behavioral task to test different hypotheses (Yang and Wang, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on RNN methodology.

claim: Shared neural modulation components in the alpha-band range (12–30 Hz) marked anticipated temporal locations.
source: We found shared neural modulation components in the alpha-band range (12–30 Hz) that marked anticipated temporal locations and were correlated with tone detection performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modulation spectrum analyses and data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The neural modulation components could not be fully explained by expectation violation or false alarms.
source: These could not be fully explained by expectation violation or false alarms.
evidence: This claim is supported by analyses shown in Figure 2I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Larger neural responses were evoked by the target tone at later temporal locations.
source: Larger neural responses were evoked by the target tone at later temporal locations.
evidence: This claim is supported by ERP data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: A significant main effect was found for Block number (F(2,34) = 5.74, p = 0.007, ηp2 = 0.252) with a significant linear trend indicating decreased tone detection performance with increasing block number (F(1,17) = 9.94, p = .006, ηp2 = 0.369).
source: A significant main effect was found for Block number (F(2,34) = 5.74, p = 0.007, ηp2 = 0.252) with a significant linear trend indicating decreased tone detection performance with increasing block number (F(1,17) = 9.94, p = .006, ηp2 = 0.369).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The decreased tone detection performance with increasing block number is attributed to participants' decreased effort or fatigue due to the repetitive trial structure in the tone detection task.
source: This effect is attributed to participants' decreased effort or fatigue due to the repetitive trial structure in the tone detection task.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral data based on inference about participant state.

claim: A significant interaction was found between Temporal location and Block number (F(4,68) = 3.80, p = .008, ηp2 = 0.183).
source: A significant interaction was found between Temporal location and Block number (F(4,68) = 3.80, p = .008, ηp2 = 0.183).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: In both ROIs, the absolute magnitude of ERPs to the target tone significantly increased with the temporal location with the ERP in the third tone location larger than the first and the second tone locations and the ERP in the second tone location larger than the first tone location (p < 0.05; adjusted FDR correction was applied).
source: In both ROIs, the absolute magnitude of ERPs to the target tone significantly increased with the temporal location with the ERP in the third tone location larger than the first and the second tone locations and the ERP in the second tone location larger than the first tone location (p < 0.05; adjusted FDR correction was applied).
evidence: This claim is supported by ERP analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Four significant modulation clusters were identified in the PMS.
source: In the PMS, four significant modulation clusters were identified, as depicted in the right plot of Figure 2B.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modulation spectrum analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Cluster 1's power frequency range falls within the delta band (1–4 Hz).
source: Cluster 1's power frequency range falls within the delta band (1–4 Hz).
evidence: This is a descriptive claim about the frequency characteristics of Cluster 1, based on data analysis.

claim: The temporal modulation trajectory of Cluster 1 mirrors the duration of the noise pieces, implying that the brain is actively monitoring the elapsed time of noise pieces and mentally registering the length of the noise piece.
source: The temporal modulation trajectory of Cluster 1 mirrors the duration of the noise pieces, implying that the brain is actively monitoring the elapsed time of noise pieces and mentally registering the length of the noise piece.
evidence: This claim is based on interpretation of the temporal dynamics of Cluster 1 shown in Figure 2D.

claim: This aligns with previous research suggesting a correlation between neural signals in the delta band or slow ramping activities and interval (or event duration) estimation.
source: This aligns with previous research suggesting a correlation between neural signals in the delta band or slow ramping activities and interval (or event duration) estimation (Breska and Deouell, 2017; van Wassenhove and Lecoutre, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on delta band activity.

claim: Significant coupling relationships post-noise onset were discovered between Clusters 2 and 3, and Clusters 3 and 4.
source: We not only confirmed the previously found coupling relationship between the delta (Cluster 1) and the beta (Cluster 2) bands (Arnal et al., 2015; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), but also discovered significant coupling relationships post-noise onset between Clusters 2 and 3, and Clusters 3 and 4.
evidence: This claim is supported by power coupling analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Clusters 2 and 4 shared the same power frequency range.
source: Furthermore, Clusters 2 and 4 shared the same power frequency range.
evidence: This is a descriptive claim about the frequency characteristics based on data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The coupling relationships and power frequency overlaps suggested that Clusters 2, 3, and 4 might collectively represent a shared neural process.
source: The coupling relationships and power frequency overlaps suggested that Clusters 2, 3, and 4 might collectively represent a shared neural process.
evidence: This is an inference based on the coupling and frequency overlap data.

claim: Cluster 1 and Cluster 234 concurrently represent the total elapsed time of the noise piece and the local temporal locations.
source: As shown in Figure 2E, Cluster 1 and Cluster 234 concurrently represent the total elapsed time of the noise piece and the local temporal locations.
evidence: This claim is supported by the temporal dynamics shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The peak latencies, relative to the corresponding temporal locations, were 0.24 s, 0.16 s, and 0.13 s, respectively.
source: After fitting a Gaussian curve to each peak, we found the peak latencies, relative to the corresponding temporal locations, to be 0.24 s, 0.16 s, and 0.13 s, respectively (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by Gaussian fitting analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: This suggests a precession of neural dynamics along the temporal locations.
source: This suggests a precession of neural dynamics along the temporal locations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the decreasing peak latencies observed in the data.

claim: The peak magnitudes of the first and second temporal locations were significantly larger than that of the third temporal location.
source: The peak magnitudes of the first and second temporal locations were significantly larger than that of the third temporal location (Figure 2I) (paired t-test: t(26) = 3.38, p=0.038; t(26) = 2.41, p=0.045).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The data show that the peak magnitude of the corrected Cluster 234 actually decreases with the temporal location, making the expectation violation explanation unlikely.
source: However, our data show that the peak magnitude of the corrected Cluster 234 actually decreases with the temporal location (Figure 2I), making the expectation violation explanation unlikely.
evidence: This claim is based on the pattern of peak magnitudes observed in the data.

claim: The peak magnitude around the first temporal location was significantly larger than the third location (t(25) = 3.04, p=0.016; adjusted FDR correction was applied).
source: The peak magnitude around the first temporal location was significantly larger than the third location (t(25) = 3.04, p=0.016; adjusted FDR correction was applied).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of peak magnitudes.

claim: These findings indicate that the block number did not interact with the neural coding of the local temporal locations, suggesting that a learning effect was not observed across blocks.
source: These findings indicate that the block number did not interact with the neural coding of the local temporal locations, suggesting that a learning effect was not observed across blocks.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical results regarding block effects.

claim: Participants quickly grasped the temporal locations of the target tone within the noise pieces and were able to anticipate these locations even in the initial block.
source: Contrary to our initial hypothesis that learning the timing of prospective moments would be a gradual process, participants quickly grasped the temporal locations of the target tone within the noise pieces. They were able to anticipate these locations even in the initial block.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral and neural data showing no learning effect across blocks.

claim: By correlating the peak magnitudes of Corrected Cluster 234 with the d-prime values, we discovered a significant positive correlation (r=0.24, p<0.001).
source: By correlating the peak magnitudes of Corrected Cluster 234 with the d-prime values (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, Figure 3C), we discovered a significant positive correlation (r=0.24, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: This indeed suggests that anticipation of the local temporal locations enhances tone detection.
source: This indeed suggests that anticipation of the local temporal locations enhances tone detection.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the positive correlation between neural markers and behavioral performance.

claim: Therefore, Corrected Cluster 234 was not a result of false alarms in the no-tone trials.
source: Therefore, Corrected Cluster 234 was not a result of false alarms in the no-tone trials.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the negative correlation between false alarms and peak magnitudes.

claim: The peak latencies at the first and second temporal locations of the second block were significantly shortened.
source: We discovered that the peak latencies at the first and second temporal locations of the second block were significantly shortened (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by permutation test results shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The peak latency significantly decreased with the temporal location.
source: The distribution of the slopes of the fitted lines indicates that the peak latency significantly decreased with the temporal location (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by permutation test results shown in Figure 3F.

claim: This observation is likely due to the sequential anticipation of the temporal locations - the anticipation of the first temporal location facilitated the anticipation of the second, and so on.
source: This observation is likely due to the sequential anticipation of the temporal locations - the anticipation of the first temporal location facilitated the anticipation of the second, and so on.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the decreasing peak latencies across temporal locations.

claim: The CRNNs, when trained to perform the same task as human participants, might also perform certain computations in a manner similar to the human brain.
source: The logic behind this is that the CRNNs, when trained to perform the same task as human participants, might also perform certain computations in a manner similar to the human brain (Yamins and DiCarlo, 2016; Yamins et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on neural network modeling.

claim: If the timing of temporal locations was expected to assist in detecting the weak target tone, the sequential temporal anticipation should be deployed more extensively at high external noise levels (low Signal-to-Noise Ratio - SNR) and less so at lower noise levels (high SNR).
source: This is because if the timing of temporal locations was expected to assist in detecting the weak target tone, the sequential temporal anticipation should be deployed more extensively at high external noise levels (low Signal-to-Noise Ratio - SNR) and less so at lower noise levels (high SNR).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about how task demands should affect neural dynamics.

claim: The modulation strength around 2 Hz increased with the external noise level used in training the CRNNs.
source: As expected, the modulation strength around 2 Hz increased with the external noise level used in training the CRNNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modulation spectra of CRNN hidden activities shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The CRNN trained at the noise level of 0.15 SD exhibited the highest modulation strength at 2 Hz, while the CRNN trained at 0.01 SD showed the least modulation strength.
source: The CRNN trained at the noise level of 0.15 SD exhibited the highest modulation strength at 2 Hz, while the CRNN trained at 0.01 SD showed the least modulation strength (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the modulation spectra shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The results showed that the dynamics of the CRNN hidden activity closely mirrored the power dynamics of Corrected Cluster 234.
source: The results showed that the dynamics of the CRNN hidden activity closely mirrored the power dynamics of Corrected Cluster 234.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The newly trained CRNN exhibited flat hidden activities devoid of any rhythmic patterns.
source: The newly trained CRNN exhibited flat hidden activities devoid of any rhythmic patterns (Figure 4F, lower panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by the CRNN hidden activities shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The tone detection performance of the newly trained CRNN dropped significantly but remained within a moderate range; in contrast, the CRNN trained with the three fixed temporal locations demonstrated superior tone detection performance at the temporal locations but much poorer performance at other time points.
source: The tone detection performance of the newly trained CRNN dropped significantly but remained within a moderate range; in contrast, the CRNN trained with the three fixed temporal locations demonstrated superior tone detection performance at the temporal locations but much poorer performance at other time points (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral performance comparison shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The findings suggest that the 2 Hz neural modulation observed in Corrected Cluster 234 served to enhance sensory sensitivity to the target tone at the anticipated temporal locations, while selectively suppressing sensory noise during irrelevant noise periods.
source: The findings presented in Figure 4F&G suggest that the 2 Hz neural modulation observed in Corrected Cluster 234 served to enhance sensory sensitivity to the target tone at the anticipated temporal locations, while selectively suppressing sensory noise during irrelevant noise periods.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the CRNN modeling results from the uniform distribution experiment.

claim: The power frequencies of Corrected Cluster 234 fall within the range typically defined as the alpha and beta bands.
source: Interestingly, the power frequencies of Corrected Cluster 234 fall within the range typically defined as the alpha and beta bands (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a descriptive claim about the frequency characteristics based on Figure 2B.

claim: Increasing evidence has shown that neural activities within these alpha-beta bands are closely associated with the suppression of internal/external noise and the regulation of information flow.
source: Increasing evidence has shown that neural activities within these alpha-beta bands are closely associated with the suppression of internal/external noise and the regulation of information flow (Arnal and Giraud, 2012; Haegens et al., 2012; Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010; Spitzer and Haegens, 2017; Wöstmann et al., 2019; Wöstmann et al., 2017; Zumer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research on alpha-beta band function.

claim: The neural findings, in conjunction with the CRNN analyses, indicate that the process of sequential temporal anticipation was partially executed as a gain control mechanism over time.
source: Our neural findings, in conjunction with the CRNN analyses, indicate that the process of sequential temporal anticipation was partially executed as a gain control mechanism over time (Salinas and Sejnowski, 2001; Strauß et al., 2014; van Ede et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a synthesis claim based on the combined neural and modeling findings.

claim: This is similar to how the brain selectively filters information for future time points, akin to the way it processes sensory information in space by focusing on attended locations and disregarding irrelevant background noise.
source: This is similar to how the brain selectively filters information for future time points, akin to the way it processes sensory information in space by focusing on attended locations and disregarding irrelevant background noise (Hillyard et al., 1998; Reynolds and Chelazzi, 2004).
evidence: This is a comparison to spatial attention mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: Previous studies have demonstrated that disrupting the balance between excitation and inhibition alters the pace of neural oscillatory activities.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that disrupting the balance between excitation and inhibition alters the pace of neural oscillatory activities (Brunel and Wang, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: When the E/I ratio fell below one (e.g. 95/105) – indicating stronger inhibitory projections and weaker excitatory ones – the peak latencies decreased with the temporal location, mirroring the neural finding.
source: When the E/I ratio fell below one (e.g. 95/105) – indicating stronger inhibitory projections and weaker excitatory ones – the peak latencies decreased with the temporal location, mirroring the neural finding shown in Figure 3E&F.
evidence: This claim is supported by the E/I perturbation results shown in Figure 4H.

claim: When the E/I ratio of the CRNN was 95/105, the behavioral performance still fell within the range of human behavioral performance.
source: We then evaluated the behavioral performance of the CRNNs with altered E/I ratios and discovered that, when the E/I ratio of the CRNN was 95/105, the behavioral performance still fell within the range of human behavioral performance (Figure 4I).
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral performance data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: The examination of E/I ratios in CRNNs suggests that the observed neural power precession in Corrected cluster 234 may be linked to enhanced neural activities of inhibitory circuits.
source: In conclusion, our examination of E/I ratios in CRNNs suggests that the observed neural power precession in Corrected cluster 234 may be linked to enhanced neural activities of inhibitory circuits.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the E/I perturbation results.

claim: The anticipations of earlier temporal locations facilitated the anticipations of subsequent ones, which is associated with the increased efficiency of inhibitory circuits.
source: The anticipations of earlier temporal locations facilitated the anticipations of subsequent ones, which is associated with the increased efficiency of inhibitory circuits.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the E/I perturbation results and the precession phenomenon.

claim: This aligns with previous neurophysiological findings and theories suggesting that neural signals in the alpha-beta bands correlate with inhibitory activities.
source: This aligns with previous neurophysiological findings and theories suggesting that neural signals in the alpha-beta bands correlate with inhibitory activities (Klimesch et al., 2007; Lakatos et al., 2016; Sherman et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on alpha-beta band function.

claim: A neural modulation component in the alpha-beta band range was utilized to locally anticipate prospective temporal locations on a sub-second scale.
source: Our research revealed that a neural modulation component in the alpha-beta band range was utilized to locally anticipate prospective temporal locations on a sub-second scale (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: The neural modulation markers for sequential temporal anticipation were found to positively correlate with the performance of tone detection.
source: The neural modulation markers for sequential temporal anticipation were found to positively correlate with the performance of tone detection (Figure 3), and these correlations could not be explained by expectation violation or false alarms.
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The neural power modulations underpinned a gain control process over time that reduced irrelevant noise periods and heightened sensory sensitivity at the anticipated temporal locations.
source: Utilizing task-optimized RNNs (Figure 4), we delved deeper into the functional role of our neural findings, demonstrating that the neural power modulations underpinned a gain control process over time that reduced irrelevant noise periods and heightened sensory sensitivity at the anticipated temporal locations.
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNN modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Temporal anticipation, a psychological term for a general task requirement, was executed in this context as a dynamic gain control process.
source: Collectively, our behavioral, neural, and neural network modeling findings suggest that temporal anticipation, a psychological term for a general task requirement, was executed in this context as a dynamic gain control process.
evidence: This is a synthesis claim based on all the findings presented in the study.

claim: The functional requirement for temporal anticipation is not only to foresee prospective moments but also to disregard irrelevant noise periods.
source: Therefore, the functional requirement for temporal anticipation is not only to foresee prospective moments but also to disregard irrelevant noise periods.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the functional requirements of temporal anticipation.

claim: Neural operations in the alpha and beta bands enhanced sensory sensitivity to the anticipated temporal locations and suppressed noise outside of these locations.
source: As shown in our neural and modeling findings, neural operations in the alpha and beta bands enhanced sensory sensitivity to the anticipated temporal locations and suppressed noise outside of these locations.
evidence: This is a summary of the neural and modeling findings regarding alpha-beta band function.

claim: This discovery aligns well with the function of attention in space – in studies of spatial attention, the alpha and beta neural bands have been found to correlate with the suppression of irrelevant objects or backgrounds.
source: This discovery aligns well with the function of attention in space – in studies of spatial attention, the alpha and beta neural bands have been found to correlate with the suppression of irrelevant objects or backgrounds (Bauer et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research on spatial attention.

claim: The precise underlying mechanisms of temporal anticipation can vary according to functional demands.
source: Our findings suggest a reinterpretation of temporal anticipation, which has often been treated as a unitary construct in various contexts (Nobre and van Ede, 2018) – the precise underlying mechanisms of temporal anticipation can vary according to functional demands.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on the findings of the study.

claim: It's plausible that the need to represent probabilities of event occurrences is influenced by task demands.
source: Therefore, it's plausible that the need to represent probabilities of event occurrences is influenced by task demands.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the RNN modeling results showing task-dependent neural dynamics.

claim: Research has shown that, on a supra-second scale, the anticipation of incoming event timings and interval estimation are primarily processed in the parietal and motor areas.
source: Regarding the brain regions involved in sequential temporal anticipation, research has shown that, on a supra-second scale, the anticipation of incoming event timings and interval estimation are primarily processed in the parietal and motor areas (Bolger et al., 2014; Coull et al., 2016; Janssen and Shadlen, 2005; Merchant and Yarrow, 2016; Morillon and Baillet, 2017; Wittmann, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research on brain regions involved in timing.

claim: Significant modulation strength was mostly observed in the EEG channels around Cz, leading to the hypothesis that the corresponding neural modulation component may originate from subcortical areas.
source: In terms of local temporal location anticipation, significant modulation strength was mostly observed in the EEG channels around Cz (Figure 2H), leading us to hypothesize that the corresponding neural modulation component may originate from subcortical areas.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the topography of neural modulation shown in Figure 2H.

claim: One potential area is the basal ganglia, particularly the striatum, which has been linked to motor sequence generation and various sub-second scale timing tasks.
source: One potential area is the basal ganglia, particularly the striatum, which has been linked to motor sequence generation and various sub-second scale timing tasks (McClure et al., 2003; Mello et al., 2015; Motanis and Buonomano, 2015; Nozaradan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on basal ganglia function.

claim: Sequential actions necessitate coordination in a series of moments, and this functional requirement aligns with the cognitive process required in our task, which is to anticipate a sequence of prospective moments.
source: As sequential actions necessitate coordination in a series of moments (Rimmele et al., 2018; Schubotz, 2007), this functional requirement aligns with the cognitive process required in our task, which is to anticipate a sequence of prospective moments.
evidence: This is a comparison between motor sequence generation and the current task, supported by citations.

claim: The brain utilizes neural power modulations across several neural bands, specifically alpha and beta, to anticipate sequential local temporal structures.
source: In conclusion, we have identified a neural processing scheme involved in sequential temporal anticipation. The brain utilizes neural power modulations across several neural bands, specifically alpha and beta, to anticipate sequential local temporal structures.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the neural findings of the study.

claim: The task-optimized artificial neural network models, particularly the RNNs, have helped uncover a dynamic gain control process that underpins temporal anticipation.
source: The task-optimized artificial neural network models, particularly the RNNs, have helped uncover a dynamic gain control process that underpins temporal anticipation.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the RNN modeling results.

claim: This process involves not only anticipating a few significant future moments, but also actively disregarding irrelevant events that frequently occur.
source: This process involves not only anticipating a few significant future moments, but also actively disregarding irrelevant events that frequently occur.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding regarding the mechanism of temporal anticipation.

claim: Thirty participants took part in the experiment (age 18–35, right-handed, 16 females).
source: Thirty participants took part in the experiment (age 18–35, right-handed, 16 females).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the participant demographics.

claim: The neurophysiological data shown in the main text included twenty-seven participants (age 18–35, right-handed, 14 females).
source: Therefore, the neurophysiological data shown in the main text included twenty-seven participants (age 18–35, right-handed, 14 females).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the final sample size for analysis.

claim: The experimental protocol was approved by the Ethics Council of the Max Planck Society.
source: The experimental protocol was approved by the Ethics Council of the Max Planck Society.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: The participants were instructed to detect a 1000 Hz pure tone of 30 ms embedded in a 2 s piece of white noise at 1 of 3 temporal locations: 500 ms, 1000 ms, and 1500 ms.
source: The participants were instructed to detect a 1000 Hz pure tone of 30 ms embedded in a 2 s piece of white noise at 1 of 3 temporal locations: 500 ms, 1000 ms, and 1500 ms.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental task.

claim: In each trial of each block, the participants were required to keep eyes open and to fix on a white cross in the center of a black screen.
source: In each trial of each block, the participants were required to keep eyes open and to fix on a white cross in the center of a black screen.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: In each of three blocks, there were four conditions: a tone appeared at either 500 ms, 1000 ms, or 1500 ms, or no tone was presented.
source: In each of three blocks, there were four conditions: a tone appeared at either 500 ms, 1000 ms, or 1500 ms, or no tone was presented.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: There were 40 trials for each condition in each block, so there were 160 trials in each of three blocks. 480 trials in total were presented.
source: There were 40 trials for each condition in each block, so there were 160 trials in each of three blocks. 480 trials in total were presented.
evidence: This is a description of the number of trials in the experiment.

claim: The white noise piece in each trial was independently generated using a random number generation function, 'rand,' in MATLAB R2016b at a sampling rate of 20,000 Hz.
source: The white noise piece in each trial was independently generated using a random number generation function, 'rand,' in MATLAB R2016b (The MathWorks, Natick, MA) at a sampling rate of 20,000 Hz.
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus generation procedure.

claim: The amplitude of white noise pieces was normalized to 70 dB SPL (sound pressure level).
source: The amplitude of white noise pieces was normalized to 70 dB SPL (sound pressure level) by referring the noise pieces to a 1-min white noise piece that was measured beforehand to be 70 dB SPL at the experimental setting.
